scope_rule: Preserve the traditional 306 clinicopathologic vocabulary and high-yield LM/IF/EM patterns, but do not let historical morphology labels become false one-to-one etiologic ontology. Pattern/entity boundaries are part of Current Knowledge quality, not an excuse to modernize away exam-relevant classifications.

source_review.primary: Current internal-medicine Lecture/AI-readable source covering primary glomerular disease, nephritic/nephrotic syndromes and case integration
source_review.external_adjudication_role: Used only where historical compression turns a pathology pattern into an unconditional disease/etiology rule; not used to expand 306 Core into a modern nephrology textbook.

findings.historical_state: B9 presents the traditional five pathology labels as a compact second coordinate alongside the clinical syndromes. This is useful for the exam but can be read as five mutually exclusive disease entities if projected without a boundary.
findings.adjudication: Keep the traditional 306 five-type pathology index for recognition and routing, but mark it as morphology/clinicopathologic pattern language rather than a complete etiologic taxonomy. In particular, mesangial proliferative, MPGN/membranoproliferative and FSGS are patterns that can arise from more than one disease mechanism; diagnosis still requires IF/EM, clinical context and cause.
findings.learning_boundary: First pass should answer two independent questions: what clinical syndrome is present, and what morphology/IF/EM pattern is present. Do not require modern etiologic subclassification beyond the stable source/exam boundary.

findings.historical_state: The source/block uses deposit location and immune-pattern shortcuts to explain why some lesions tend toward nephritic/inflammatory vs nephrotic/permeability phenotypes.
findings.adjudication: Preserve the mechanistic tendency: subendothelial/endocapillary inflammatory exposure tends to produce nephritic inflammation, while subepithelial/podocyte-side injury more often produces heavy proteinuria. But this is not a deterministic lookup table; the same clinicopathologic entity can overlap syndromes and evolve over time.

findings.historical_state: Traditional RPGN type-III shorthand strongly couples pauci-immune crescentic GN with ANCA-associated vasculitis and can collapse the relationship into 'type III = ANCA positive'.
findings.adjudication: Current Core should teach type III as pauci-immune crescentic GN, commonly associated with ANCA-associated vasculitis. ANCA-negative pauci-immune GN exists, so ANCA positivity is high-value supporting/etiologic evidence rather than a logical requirement of the pauci-immune morphology.
findings.learning_boundary: For 306, retain the high-yield triad: type I anti-GBM/linear, type II immune-complex/granular, type III pauci-immune/often ANCA-associated. Do not expand the full vasculitis taxonomy here.

findings.historical_state: The traditional exam route strongly associates IgA nephropathy with mesangial proliferation and can be read as a fixed LM identity.
findings.adjudication: The stable diagnostic pathology Core is mesangial-dominant/co-dominant IgA on immunofluorescence with mesangial/paramesangial deposits on EM. Light microscopy is variable: mesangial hypercellularity/proliferation is common, but LM can range from minimal change-like appearances to segmental sclerosis or crescentic injury. Do not encode IgA nephropathy as identical to one LM pattern.
findings.learning_boundary: Keep 'mesangial proliferation is typical/high-yield' for 306 recognition; IF IgA dominance is the stronger identity anchor. Full Oxford MEST-C prognostic scoring is not required unless the Current exam source explicitly owns it.

findings.historical_state: B11 teaches MCD, membranous, mesangial proliferative, MPGN and FSGS as the traditional nephrotic pathology comparison set. That is exam-useful, but MsPGN/MPGN/FSGS can be misread as single-cause disease entities.
findings.adjudication: Preserve the classic 306 LM/IF/EM and age/treatment tendencies, but mark MsPGN, MPGN and FSGS as morphology/clinicopathologic patterns whose etiology can be primary or secondary depending on context. MPGN in particular is a pattern that modern classification re-organizes by immune-complex vs complement-mediated mechanisms; FSGS can be primary, genetic or secondary. The exam table remains a recognition index, not a complete etiologic ontology.
findings.learning_boundary: Do not replace the 306 table with modern guideline taxonomy. Add one explicit boundary before/inside the comparison so the learner can later absorb etiologic classification without unlearning the morphology.

findings.historical_state: Traditional tables attach steroid sensitivity/resistance tendencies directly to pathology labels, especially MCD vs FSGS.
findings.adjudication: Keep the exam tendency: MCD is typically steroid-responsive and primary FSGS is often less responsive. But treatment logic must not be generalized from the FSGS lesion alone because secondary/adaptive/genetic FSGS is not the same immunosuppressive owner as primary FSGS.
